title: Gen. Shanahan Remarks | 'Mitigating the Risks of AI Integration in Nuclear Operations'
summary: Gen. Jack Shanahan argues the biggest AI risks to nuclear operations come from faster decision cycles, automation bias, epistemic capture, data poisoning and rogue AI agents rather than direct launch authority.

assertions.quote: The 2024 Biden she agreement that humans should retain control over nuclear use decisions was an important starting point.
risks associated with dramatically accelerating nuclear decision timelines or reducing meaningful human involvement in launch decisions and execution are likely to outweigh the benefits
AI changing the information environment, accelerating decision cycles, shaping what commanders believe to be true
Epistemic capture occurs when an AI systems representation of reality becomes so dominant that the human can no longer recognize it

verdicts.note: Automation bias is well documented in military and civilian settings, though its effect on nuclear decisions is untested.

RAND warns that for decision-support systems it is especially dangerous for the side using the AI to believe it works when it does not, and that experts fear over-reliance could cause catastrophic mistakes.
SIPRI says decision makers may become overly dependent on AI recommendations, mistaking algorithmic suggestions for their own judgement (automation bias).

CNAS warns that automation bias and the history of false alarms in early-warning systems mean AI decision aids in warning and forecasting should be adopted with caution, the route by which over-reliance could mislead nuclear decisions.

The Bulletin notes AI may be embedded in nuclear decision-support systems and warns that too-heavy dependence on black-box systems could be a serious danger even with a human deciding; expert judgment.

assertions.quote: surprisingly small amounts of deliberative deliberately manipulated data can poison large language models or skew their behavior

verdicts.note: Data-poisoning attacks on models are demonstrated in research, but doing it to classified military systems is harder and undocumented.

RAND warns an adversary could manipulate an AI's inputs, for example by mobilizing forces in a set pattern, so that it judges an incoming strike safe, and that such attacks do not need access to the system.
SIPRI says corrupting the training data of AI decision-support systems could skew outputs toward dangerous decisions in nuclear command systems, and a cyber operation could do so deliberately.
WEF warns adversaries might poison military AI training data as a covert weapon; it supports manipulation of military AI in general but does not tie it to nuclear decisions.

assertions.quote: An autonomous AI agent could become a third-party catalyst in a nuclear crisis without ever gaining access to a nuclear weapon

verdicts.note: A speculative scenario with no precedent; current agents lack the autonomy and access it assumes.
SIPRI notes AI deepfakes and disinformation spread during the May 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, with possible nuclear consequences, but does not describe an autonomous AI agent provoking a crisis.

WEF says weaponized generative AI can fabricate executive orders or convincing battlefield footage that confuses humans and automated responses; that supports fabrication as a crisis risk but not a rogue agent or a nuclear crisis specifically.

assertions.quote: Maintaining human control, protecting decision authority, managing entanglement
